newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian recovery hopes focus on new cabinet.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian recovery hopes focus on new cabinet.

text.p: Bulgaria's new reformist cabinet appointed by parliament on Wednesday faces a challenge to live up to high public expectations and complete market reforms delayed since the end of communist rule, officials say.

"The new government will have difficulty in fulfilling radical reforms and resisting populist measures. The expectations lavished on it may turn against it if it fails to fulfill pledges," said one Western diplomat.

"I have no illusions for what lies ahead. It is very hard, but we are full of will and confidence," Ivan Kostov, leader of the reformist Union of Democratic Forces (UDF), told reporters after the 240-seat parliament approved his cabinet.
Kostov, finance minister in two previous governments in 1991 and 1992, led the UDF to victory in last month's elections after widespread civil violence ousted the Socialists from power in February.

His cabinet, the 10th since Bulgaria embarked on the transition to a market economy after the collapse of the communist regime in 1989, is expected to overhaul the economy, crack down on corruption and organised crime and increase foreign investment.

One of its first tasks will be to introduce an IMF-prescribed currency board system, known as a restrictive fixed exchange rate regime designed to stabilise the shaky banking system and volatile currency.
Kostov said priorities would also be to speed up privatisations, close inefficient and loss-making state enterprises and sell state banks preferably to foreign strategic investors by the end of 1998.
He said the government must also organise safety nets for those affected by such restructuring.
The Pari daily commented: "The new cabinet will be attacked for its privatisation deals, its social policy and on NATO memberhsip."
Socialist deputies, widely blamed by Bulgarians for the country's economic near-collapse, voted against the new government accusing it of being a single party cabinet.
The Socialists' ambiguous views on foreign investment, privatisation and NATO membership, which they feared would ubset Russia, led to an unprecedented economic crisis and isolation last year.
Kostov pledged full openness in government and told his ministers to suspend any private business dealings to prevent a conflict of interests.

The UDF has strong support from the small Euroleft coalition which includes prominent Socialist dissidents and more guarded support from the Union for National Salvation, which includes ethnic Turks and monarchists.

"This cabinet will meet people's expectations if it succeeds in battling crime and corruption, sets clear banking regulations, restores confidence and raises living standards," said President Petar Stoyanov.
Stoyanov praised the previous interim cabinet for its legacy to the new government.

In its three months in office, the interim cabinet is credited with negotiating a $657 million accord with the International Monetary Fund to stabilise the national currency, bringing grain and fuel shortages under control and freeing prices and trade rules for most goods.
"The new cabinet has chances to succeed..." said the Standart daily in an editorial "It openly declared that the cost of transition will not be low, but there is no other way to avoid misery."
